n November 4, 2026, between 09:35 UTC and 11:43 UTC, customers experienced intermittent errors and timeouts across GitHub.com, primarily on actions that write data. Reads were largely unaffected, and retrying a failed action a short time later usually succeeded.The incident was triggered by a burst of concurrent updates to the same database record, which tied up all available connections to one of our primary databases. Although that contention cleared, the backlog of waiting requests kept our database connection layer overloaded, and it did not recover on its own. We mitigated the incident by failing over to a new primary database host. Most services recovered by 11:31 UTC, and Actions recovered by 11:43 UTC.Since the incident, we have disabled the code path that triggered the contention, increased the processing capacity of our database connection layer by 50%, and added alerting to detect this type of overload earlier. We are also improving our procedures so we can fail over sooner in similar situations.

On November 9, 2026, between 18:07 and 18:59 UTC, GitHub Actions experienced degraded performance. During this time, some customers saw workflow runs fail to start, update or report status correctly. An average of 28% of workflow runs were affected, peaking at 65% during the worst period of the incident. Once Actions services recovered, some jobs were left in a state that limited available concurrency until the runs were released. The incident occurred during a planned migration of a core Actions database from GitHub’s datacenter to a new cloud region. After the migration completed, we shifted Actions service traffic to the new region. The volume of requests exceeded the capacity and rate limits configured there, so a portion of requests were rejected and workflow updates failed. Dependent services, including Webhooks, Pages and Copilot code review, saw secondary impact. We mitigated impact by shifting some of the traffic back to the original region, allowing service traffic to remain within the configured limits. We then increased capacity and rate limits in the new region before gradually shifting traffic back. While this was a one-time migration event for this cluster that is now complete, we are improving how we validate capacity and limits before shifting traffic during remaining migrations, including shifting traffic in smaller steps. To address the stuck runs left after the incident, we are improving our ability to detect and mitigate these runs for future cases as well as readying an API to enable customers to address this themselves.

Some pull requests continued to display an earlier source-branch commit after the broader service degradation ended. The degradation resulted from overload in the shared infrastructure that supports Git operations. Recent changes increased background processing and the work required to compute pull request merges, adding pressure to the same systems used by customer-facing requests. We mitigated the incident by disabling a recent merge-processing optimization, pausing background analysis, and temporarily limiting lower-priority traffic. The temporary limits also restricted access to commit pages for users who were not signed in. Background processing continued to catch up after service health recovered. We have reduced repeated repository-analysis work and are adding workload-level concurrency controls to better protect customer-facing requests. We are also improving our procedures for safely reducing background load and making pull request synchronization more resilient to temporary failures.

On November 25, 2026, between 21:30 UTC and 00:28 UTC, Git Large File Storage (LFS) operations on github.com were degraded. During this time, an average of 2% of Git LFS requests failed, peaking at 4%. Many more requests initially failed but succeeded when Git LFS clients automatically retried them, which caused slower uploads and downloads for affected users. Other Git operations were not affected. This was due to a large volume of automated, unauthenticated traffic that overwhelmed the Git LFS servers in one of our regions, leaving them unable to respond to requests in time.We mitigated the incident by moving most Git LFS traffic from the affected region to other regions with more capacity. Error rates returned to normal by 00:28 UTC.We are working to limit the impact of high-volume unauthenticated traffic on Git LFS, and to add capacity in the affected region, to prevent similar disruptions in the future.
